input.question: Why does pinching a hose at its extremity make the water flow faster while pinching in the middle make the water flow weaker?
input.ground_truth: because it reduces the volume moving past that point while increasing the speed due to the pressure behind. When you pinch in the middle, the volume is restricted, but then expanded again, meaning the rest of the hose has reduced pressure and volume, due to the expanded area. If you keep the hose pinched all the way along from the first pinch point to the end, the water will flow faster (but you'll have increased friction all along that stretch which will slow things down a bit).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why does pinching a hose at its extremity make the water flow faster while pinching in the middle make the water flow weaker?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the hose is like a straw with water inside. 

If you pinch the very end of the straw (the extremity), the water has only a tiny space to come out. It has to squeeze through that tiny spot, so it comes out really fast—like when you put your thumb over the end of a water gun!

But if you pinch the hose in the middle, you are stopping the water from going through a big part of the straw. Now the water behind the pinch wants to go forward, but it can’t get past the pinch. So, it can only squeeze out a little bit at a time, and it comes out slower.

So, pinching at the end makes a small hole for the water to rush out fast. Pinching in the middle blocks a lot of the water, so it can only trickle out slowly!
